t.2.63.1: On the very night that those messengers entered that city, Bharata too, on that same night, saw this unpleasant dream.
t.2.63.3: Perceiving him to be tormented, his sweet-spoken companions, intending to dispel his distress, began conversations in the assembly hall.
t.2.63.2: But as that night was just breaking into dawn, the son of the king of kings, having seen that unpleasant dream, was exceedingly tormented.
t.2.63.4: Some played soothing music, and others had dances performed; still others recited dramas and various comic pieces.
t.2.63.5: Though those sweet-spoken friends made merry jests in their gathering, the great-souled Bharata, the Rāghava, did not rejoice.
t.2.63.6: A dear friend, seated among well-wishers, said to Bharata, who was surrounded by companions: “Friend, why do you not rejoice?”
t.2.63.7: To his friend, who was speaking thus, Bharata replied: "Listen to the cause for which this dejection has come upon me."
t.2.63.8: In a dream I saw my father, soiled and with his hair let loose, falling from the summit of a mountain into a foul pool of cow dung.
t.2.63.9: And he was seen by me floating in that pool of cow dung, drinking oil from his cupped hands and laughing, as it were, again and again.
t.2.63.10: Then, having eaten rice cooked with sesame, his whole body anointed with oil, he plunged again and again, head downward, into oil itself.
t.2.63.11: In a dream I saw the ocean dried up, the moon fallen to the earth, and blazing Jātavedas, the fire, suddenly extinguished.
t.2.63.12: I see the earth split open, and trees of many kinds withered, and the mountains shattered and wreathed in smoke.
t.2.63.13: And women, dark and tawny, were laughing at the king as he sat on a seat of black iron, clad in black garments.
t.2.63.14: And the righteous-souled one, adorned with red garlands and smeared with red unguents, was hastening away on a chariot yoked with donkeys, setting out with his face turned toward the south.
t.2.63.15: This is what I saw during this fearful night: either I, or Rāma, or the king, or Lakṣmaṇa will die.
t.2.63.16: For the man who in a dream rides in a carriage yoked with donkeys, before long the tip of the smoke from his funeral pyre is seen. Because of this I am downcast, and so I do not return your courtesies.
t.2.63.17: My throat seems to be drying up, and my mind seems unsettled; I seem almost to loathe myself, yet I see no reason for it.
t.2.63.18: Having witnessed the course of this evil dream, so manifold and never imagined before, that great fear does not leave my heart as I think of the king, whom I saw in a form beyond all imagining.
